newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU proposes tax on international callbacks.
newsitem.headline: EU proposes tax on international callbacks.

text.p: The European Commission proposed legislation Wednesday that would slap a consumption tax on telecommunications services offered by foreign companies within the 15-nation European Union.

The initiative was prompted by the growing popularity of "callback" services operating in the United States, which allow consumers to bypass high European telecommunications costs by routing their calls through U.S. phone lines.
Those calls are not now subject to national value-added taxes (VAT), which range from 15 percent in Luxembourg and Germany to 25 percent in Denmark and Sweden.

The commission, responding to a unanimous request from EU governments, proposed that foreign firms be required to charge VAT on telecommunications services offered to EU customers -- putting them on a par with their European counterparts.
"These proposals aim to eliminate the unfair advantage enjoyed now by third-country service providers," EU Taxation Commissioner Mario Monti said in a statement.

The proposal, which must be agreed unanimously by EU finance ministers, would not apply to Internet or online services when the consumer connects through a local phone call, Alexander Wiedow, an official in the commission's taxation division, told reporters.

He said an early draft of the commission's proposal would have imposed the value-added tax on some "broadcast" services, but was revised to conform with a narrower definition of telecommunications that the EU is advocating in World Trade Organisation talks on telecommunications liberalisation.
With callback services, a customer can dial a number, usually in the United States, and get called back with an open line to phone anywhere in the world -- at low U.S. rates.
A spokeswoman in the Brussels office of AT&T Corp., which operates a "callback" service known as AT&T International Call Plan, was sanguine about the commission's initiative.
"We're committed to the European marketplace and will abide by its regulations," Valerie Hasselbach said in an interview. She added that callback services represented a "huge market."
But unlike AT&T, many callback services operate only from the United States, raising the question of how the EU could enforce the value-added-tax charges.
Wiedow said U.S. companies had informed the commission they were willing to comply with the rules as long as they had enough time to prepare.
Once the regime is fully in place, envisaged for the start of 1999, callback operators will be required to register in an EU country and to collect and pay the value-added-tax themselves.
